ta-l1d28q1-d1e97.summary: A divisio textus for Distinction 28. Lombard treats the notions of the persons that are not personal: first innascibility, a property of a person but not a personal property, then 'principle', which is neither (Dist. 29). He shows how the Father is called unbegotten, expounding the term with examples, raising whether only the Father should be called 'not begotten', identifying from Hilary the notion the name designates, and noting the Arians' argument from it to a difference of substance. He then shows that, as only the Son is called Word or Image, only he is called born or begotten Wisdom, removing two doubts, including that 'image' is sometimes said according to substance. Thomas asks about innascibility and about image; on innascibility, whether it is a notion or property of the Father, and whether it is his personal property. Whether 'unbegotten' fits the Spirit was settled in Dist. 13.
claims: Innascibility is a property of the Father but not a personal property.
Only the Son is called begotten Wisdom, Word, and Image.

ta-l1d28q1-d1e143.summary: First argument that innascibility is not a notion or property of the Father. The text says 'unbegotten' shows not what he is but what he is not, and a negation cannot sufficiently make something known, while a notion is the principle of knowing a person.
claims: Negation cannot make a person known.

ta-l1d28q1-d1e146.summary: Second argument. If 'unbegotten' is the Father's property, it is so negatively or privatively. Not negatively, since then it fits whatever is not begotten, including the essence and the Spirit; not privatively, since privation always implies imperfection, being the lack of what is naturally apt to be had.
claims: Negatively it is too broad; privatively it implies imperfection.

ta-l1d28q1-d1e149.summary: Third argument. Since the persons are distinguished only by relations, nothing outside the genus of relation can be a notion. 'Unbegotten' is not in that genus: as inferior relates to superior, the negation of the superior relates to that of the inferior conversely (non-animal is narrower than non-man), and generation as relation is narrower than relation, so non-generation is more common than non-relation and holds of it as common of proper. What holds with the opposite of a genus is not within the genus.
claims: The negation of generation extends to what is non-relation, so it is outside the genus of relation.

ta-l1d28q1-d1e153.summary: Fourth argument. 'Unbegotten' fits the Father as principle, and he is principle by both generation and spiration, so he should be made known by denying procession in general ('improcessible') or by denying each procession ('unbegotten' and 'unspirable').
claims: The Father should be called improcessible or unspirable too.

ta-l1d28q1-d1e156.summary: Sed contra from Hilary in the text.
claims: Hilary treats unbegottenness as the Father's property.

ta-l1d28q1-d1e159.summary: Second sed contra. What distinguishes a divine person from the others is his notion or property, and 'unbegotten' fits only the Father (Dist. 13).
claims: Only the Father is unbegotten.

ta-l1d28q1-d1e162.summary: Thomas's determination. According to Augustine the Father is the principle of the whole divinity, and Dionysius says the fount of divinity is in the Father. If the persons had an order of prior and posterior, the Father would be the first principle, but since they do not, in place of 'first' we say 'principle not from a principle'. So the Father can be made known in two ways: as not from a principle, by the notion of innascibility, and as principle, by two notions according to the two modes of emanation from him, paternity as principle by generation and common spiration as principle of the Spirit by spiration of love. So the Father has three notions in all.
claims: The Father is 'principle not from a principle', in place of 'first principle'.
The Father has three notions: innascibility, paternity, and common spiration.

ta-l1d28q1-d1e165.summary: Reply to the first argument. A word posits something in two ways: as of its concept, part of its essence, as 'man' posits animal; or as presupposed as its foundation, though not of its essence, as every accident posits substance. 'Unbegotten' posits nothing constituting its concept, since that could only be a character of principle, general or special, the only notional thing that can fit the Father, and then innascibility would not be counted with paternity, since the common is not counted with the proper. But it posits something it presupposes as its foundation, which is why some said it posits something and others nothing. Though it posits nothing constitutive, it can still be a notion, since what consists in removal is best made known by negation, like blindness, and such is the character of the first, or of being not from a principle, since the first is that before which there is nothing.
claims: 'Unbegotten' posits nothing constitutively but presupposes the character of principle as its foundation.
What consists in removal is best made known by negation.

ta-l1d28q1-d1e168.summary: Reply to the second argument. 'Unbegotten' implies not absolute negation but in some way privation, since every negation in a determinate subject can be called privation (Metaphysics 8: privation is negation in a subject). Its negation is understood as founded on the character of principle, as the Father's notion, and so fits neither the essence nor the Spirit, who are not principle by origin of a divine person, nor the Son, who has the opposite affirmation. No imperfection follows, since privation, of what is naturally apt to be had, is said three ways (Metaphysics 5): when something lacks what anything is apt to have, though it is not apt (a foot lacks sight); when it lacks what its genus is apt to have, though not it or its species (a mole lacks sight); and when it lacks what it is apt to have, when and where and so on, which is privation proper and implies imperfection. In this last way nothing is said privatively of God, but the first two can be. In the first way 'unbegotten' can be said of the essence and the Spirit, as Jerome takes it (Dist. 13), and in the second only of the Father, since he is a notional principle without the passive generation the Son has, who is also a notional principle.
claims: 'Unbegotten' is a quasi-privation founded on the character of principle, without imperfection.
Of three senses of privation, only the strict one implies imperfection, and it is not said of God.

ta-l1d28q1-d1e172.summary: Reply to the third argument. Something is in a genus per se and properly, like species and what receive the genus's predication, or by reduction, like the principles of a genus (matter and form to substance, unity and point to quantity). No negation or privation is per se in a genus, having no quiddity or being, but is reduced to the genus of the affirmation, since being is understood in non-being and affirmation in negation, every privation known by its habit and removal by position. So even non-relation is in the genus of relation by reduction, though the things it is said of are not in that genus.
claims: Negations are in the genus of their affirmation by reduction.

ta-l1d28q1-d1e175.summary: Reply to the fourth argument. 'Unbegotten' removes from the Father being from another simply, not only in some determinate mode. That he is named by denying the special procession of generation has three reasons. First, the Spirit's procession presupposes the Son's generation by order of nature, so denying the prior removes the posterior: removing generation from the fontal principle removes procession by love. Second, 'unbegotten', as the Father's notion, removes every way of following generation, which belongs to the Father as principle of generation; something follows generation as begotten (the Son), as received through generation (the divine essence), or as proceeding from the begotten (the Spirit), so 'unbegotten' in this sense fits none of them. Third, the negation in 'unbegotten' is founded on the character of principle, and though the Father is principle of both processions, only the character by which he is principle of generation, paternity, is his personal property constituting him, so he is more fittingly made known by negating generation.
claims: 'Unbegotten' removes being from another simply.
It is named from generation because spiration presupposes generation, because it excludes everything following generation, and because paternity is the Father's constituting property.
concepts: ingenitus as negation of esse ab alio

ta-l1d28q1-d1e187.summary: First argument that innascibility is the Father's personal property. Like paternity, it belongs only to the Father, and paternity is his personal property.
claims: Innascibility is proper to the Father like paternity.

ta-l1d28q1-d1e190.summary: Second argument. A person is distinguished by a property of dignity, and innascibility seems more dignified than paternity, since paternity is communicated to creatures and innascibility is not.
claims: Innascibility is more dignified than paternity.

ta-l1d28q1-d1e193.summary: Third argument. A person cannot be understood without what constitutes him in his personhood, and the text says the unbegotten can be understood even without understanding the Father, so innascibility constitutes the Father's person.
claims: The unbegotten can be understood without the Father.

ta-l1d28q1-d1e197.summary: Fourth argument. The principle of a personal operation seems to be a personal property, since a proper operation comes from the agent's proper form, and innascibility is the principle of generation in the Father, since it is said that the Father begets because he is unbegotten, seeking delight in the Son's companionship.
claims: The Father begets because he is unbegotten.

ta-l1d28q1-d1e200.summary: Sed contra. What is said positively is not constituted only negatively or privatively, and 'Father' names something positive, so his person is not constituted by innascibility, which posits nothing in its concept.
claims: A positive person is not constituted by negation.

ta-l1d28q1-d1e203.summary: Thomas's determination. As in lower things whatever follows complete being does not constitute the thing, in God whatever presupposes conceptually that by which a person is constituted cannot constitute the person. So common spiration is not a personal property, since it presupposes active and passive generation, which constitute Father and Son. Likewise innascibility, positing a negation founded on the character of principle, presupposes that character, paternity, conceptually, so it cannot constitute the Father's person or be a personal property.
claims: What conceptually presupposes the constituting property cannot be personal.
Innascibility and common spiration presuppose paternity and generation, so they are not personal properties.

ta-l1d28q1-d1e206.summary: Reply to the first argument. Belonging only to the Father proves it is a property of the Father, not a personal property, unless it constituted his person like a constitutive difference.
claims: Being proper does not make a property personal.

ta-l1d28q1-d1e209.summary: Reply to the second argument. Whatever dignity a negation has it has from the affirmation it is founded on, so innascibility, founded on such paternity, pertains to dignity as that paternity does; and as innascibility is not communicated to creatures, neither is such paternity, paternity not from another principle, though paternity as such is.
claims: Innascibility's dignity derives from unoriginated paternity.

ta-l1d28q1-d1e212.summary: Reply to the third argument. With paternity removed in thought, the Father's hypostasis does not remain. The text's statement that 'unbegotten' remains concerns the common concepts of unbegotten and father, which are found separately in different things, not as both are properties of the Father. Still, with paternity removed, 'unbegotten' would remain in God not as a property or notion of a person but as an attribute of the essence, like 'immense' and 'uncreated'.
claims: Without paternity, unbegottenness would remain only as an essential attribute.

ta-l1d28q1-d1e216.summary: Reply to the fourth argument. Innascibility is the principle of generation in the Father not as the form eliciting the operation but only as setting a condition on it. As the first alteration is the one done by an alterer that is not altered, being first because the alterer is unaltered, so the first generation is that of a begetter not begotten, which has the condition of being first because the begetter is unbegotten. The formal principle eliciting generation is the Father's form, paternity, as heat is the principle of heating in the hot.
claims: Innascibility conditions generation as first; paternity is its formal principle.

ta-l1d28q1-Dd1e92.summary: The Prooemium of Distinction 28 divides Lombard's treatment of non-personal notions, innascibility and (in Dist. 29) 'principle', and of the Son as begotten Wisdom and Image. It announces two questions, on innascibility and on image, and two articles on the first: whether innascibility is a notion of the Father, and whether it is his personal property.
claims: Innascibility is a non-personal notion.

ta-l1d28q1-Dd1e135.summary: Article 1 holds that innascibility is a notion and property of the Father, who, there being no prior and posterior in God, is 'principle not from a principle' and is known by three notions: innascibility, paternity, and common spiration. 'Unbegotten' posits nothing constitutively but presupposes the character of principle, and what consists in removal is best known by negation. It is a quasi-privation founded on that character, implying no imperfection, and belongs to the genus of relation by reduction. It removes being from another simply, but is named from generation because spiration presupposes generation and paternity is the Father's constituting property.
claims: Innascibility is a notion of the Father, a negation founded on his being principle.
The Father has three notions.

ta-l1d28q1-Dd1e179.summary: Article 2 holds that innascibility is not the Father's personal property. Whatever conceptually presupposes the constituting property cannot constitute the person, and innascibility, founded on paternity, presupposes it, as common spiration presupposes generation. Its dignity derives from unoriginated paternity; without paternity it would remain only as an essential attribute; and it conditions generation as first, while paternity is its formal principle.
claims: Innascibility is a property of the Father but not personal, since it presupposes paternity.

ta-l1d28q1.summary: Quaestio 1 of Book I, Distinction 28 treats innascibility. Article 1 holds that it is a notion of the Father, who as principle not from a principle is known by innascibility, paternity, and common spiration. 'Unbegotten' is a negation, a quasi-privation without imperfection founded on the character of principle and reduced to the genus of relation. Article 2 holds that innascibility is not a personal property, since it presupposes paternity, which alone constitutes the Father and is the formal principle of generation.
claims: Innascibility is a notion of the Father, founded on his being principle.
It is not a personal property, since it presupposes paternity.
